narrative:
The model estimates an 85% chance that you will leave your current job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This high probability reflects patterns the system sees in your overall profile compared to others who tend to stay.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this outlook, in order of importance, were your total years of professional experience, the length of time you have spent in your current role, and the fact that you have received other job offers while working here. 

Your 6–10 years of overall experience pushed the prediction toward leaving. While many employees predicted to stay have shorter careers (1–5 years is most common among stayers), your mid-level experience appears to align more with people who eventually move on. Similarly, having spent 1–5 years in this organization also contributed to the “will leave” direction, as this tenure bracket is typical for those who start looking elsewhere once they have gained some familiarity with the role. Finally, receiving external job opportunities strongly increased the likelihood of departure; only about one in four employees predicted to stay report having such offers, whereas you do.

Taken together, these elements suggest the model sees you as someone with enough experience to be marketable and who is already receiving outside interest. The organization should consider discussing retention measures with you, such as clearer promotion paths or improved recognition of your contributions. You may wish to reflect on whether your current role still aligns with your longer-term goals.
